where: Section 1, sentence after the ρ0 definition
problem: The sentence "At low speed, q = ½ρV², so the same q gives a lower true speed in thin air" has the physics backwards. From V = √(2q/ρ), a fixed q with a smaller ρ gives a LARGER true speed, not a smaller one. The exam traps section itself says the opposite ("the same IAS corresponds to a higher TAS because the air density is lower"), so a student sees two contradicting statements.
fix: "Rearranging q = ½ρV² gives V = √(2q/ρ). The dial is calibrated at ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³, so a given q always shows the same indicated speed. In thin air ρ is smaller, so the same q is produced by a higher true speed: TAS is greater than IAS, and the gap grows with altitude."

where: Section 1, definitions of CAS and TAS
problem: "True airspeed (TAS) corrects IAS for density" skips CAS and ignores compressibility, so the chain IAS → CAS → TAS is loose and the two corrections look like one.
fix: "Calibrated airspeed (CAS) is IAS corrected for position and installation error. True airspeed (TAS) is CAS corrected for air density, and at high Mach number also for compressibility."

problem: q = P0 − P = ½ρV² is written as if it always holds. It is the incompressible form, valid only below roughly Mach 0.3; above that the relation between impact pressure and speed changes and the ASI needs a compressibility correction.
fix: Add one line: "q = ½ρV² holds for incompressible flow, roughly below Mach 0.3 (about 200 kt at sea level); at higher speed the airspeed indicator needs a compressibility correction."

problem: Fuel quantity indication is usually capacitive or float based, not a pressure-to-reading chain; only some systems (for example pressure or density sensors in a tank) work from pressure, so the flat comparison can mislead.
fix: "Some pressure-sensing chains also appear in fuel quantity indication, see 3.13."
